name: The Royal Oaks of Lazienki

location.address: Lazienki Krolewskie park, near the New Orangery, west side of the Chinska Droga path, Srodmiescie

access: Free, the park gardens are open daily to the public at no charge (only some buildings/museum interiors are ticketed)
transport: Bus or tram to Lazienki Krolewskie, short walk within the park to the New Orangery area
verify_notes: Two pedunculate oaks, officially designated a natural monument (pomnik przyrody) 1974-08-20, INSPIRE code PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1465011.2994, GDOS register + Polish Wikipedia's reproduction of the city's official monuments list both place them near the New Orangery, west side of the Chinska Droga path, inside Lazienki Krolewskie park (Poland's best-known royal park, laid out for King Stanislaw August Poniatowski in the 18th century). Second, independent source: Lazienki Museum's own official page 'The oldest trees of the Royal Lazienki' (lazienki-krolewskie.pl) states 'for almost two centuries, two specimen of the European oak have grown in the Romantic Garden. They are 450 centimetres in circumference and 28 metres high. Both are precious natural monuments.' Girth 450cm supports the museum's own ~200-year estimate for a pedunculate oak on good soil. Flagging one honest wrinkle for the writer: the museum page names the location 'Romantic Garden' while the register names 'near the New Orangery, west side of Chinska Droga' - both are real, closely-sited features inside the same park and very likely the same pair of trees (both sources independently describe exactly two old pedunculate oaks as protected monuments, and no other oak pair is recorded in Lazienki), but no single source states the equivalence explicitly, so do not assert it as fact beyond 'in or near the Romantic Garden by the New Orangery.' Alive: no removal/status-revoked note in Wikipedia's list (which does record other trees in the same list as fallen/delisted, e.g. Sowinski's Linden below), and the museum's own 2026-dated page describes them in present tense as currently growing. Story angle: two centuries in the garden of Poland's last king, inside the country's most visited royal park, girth thick enough (450cm) to have been substantial trees already when Poland lost its independence in the partitions. Register+Wikipedia list count as one source family per project convention; the Lazienki Museum's own page is the independent second source for age and girth.

name: King Jan's Linden

location.address: Wilanow palace park, south side of the main avenue leading to the palace, about 25m from ul. Wiertnicza, ul. Stanislawa Kostki Potockiego 10/16, Wilanow

access: Paid entry to the Wilanow palace park grounds (Museum of King Jan III's Palace in Wilanow); check current ticket prices, some days offer free entry to parts of the site
transport: Bus to Wilanow, short walk into the palace park grounds
verify_notes: Small-leaved lime, officially designated a natural monument 1975-01-31, INSPIRE code PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1465011.3470, standing on the south side of the main avenue leading to Wilanow Palace, about 25m from ul. Wiertnicza. Second, independent source: Wilanow Palace Museum's own page 'Drzewa pomnikowe w Wilanowie' confirms 28 monument trees inventoried in the palace gardens across 6 genera including lipa (Tilia sp.), of which 27 are living in good physiological condition and one is dead with its crown removed; the page does not single out this specific linden's own dimensions, so I cannot independently confirm which of the 27 living ones it is beyond the register's own coordinate and INSPIRE match. Some search results (not independently verified against a live primary source in this pass; the specific monument subpage returned 404 when fetched directly) report a girth 'exceeding 4 metres' and height 'over 20 metres' for this tree, so treat that figure as unconfirmed and worth a follow-up fetch rather than as sourced fact. Naming: local/museum tradition calls it 'King Jan's Linden' after Jan III Sobieski, who built Wilanow and is documented (general historical accounts of the gardens) to have personally planted lindens there; no source ties THIS SPECIFIC tree to a Sobieski-era planting date, so age_estimate is left undocumented rather than bridging the general legend to this one specimen, per the bridge-claim trap. Alive: the museum's own inventory page states 27 of 28 monument trees in these gardens are alive in good condition and only one is dead (crown fully removed, which would be conspicuous and is not how this linden is described anywhere); no source describes this specific linden as dead or removed.

name: Niemcewicz's Walnut

location.address: Grounds of the Krasinski Palace (Palac Krasinskich), ul. Nowoursynowska 166, SGGW campus, Ursynow

access: Free. The palace's terraced garden behind the building, where the tree stands, has been open to the public daily from April to October, 8am-6pm, since SGGW opened it to visitors in 2025 (closed on internal-event or bad-weather days); the tree itself grows by the palace on the open campus grounds
transport: Metro or bus to Ursynow (SGGW campus, Nowoursynowska 166), short walk to the Krasinski Palace
verify_notes: Black walnut, officially designated a natural monument, INSPIRE code PL.ZIPOP.1393.PP.1465011.3472, growing by the Krasinski Palace (Palac Krasinskich, also called Palac Rozkosz) on the SGGW campus at ul. Nowoursynowska 166. Second, independent source: Polish Wikipedia's own article on the Krasinski Palace (distinct from the citywide monuments-list article) confirms 'Przy palacu rosnie Drzewo Niemcewicza - orzech czarny (Juglans nigra), bedacy pomnikiem przyrody' (By the palace grows Niemcewicz's Tree, a black walnut, a natural monument), itself citing Warsaw city hall's own BIP register of natural monuments. Naming and history: the palace was owned from 1822 by Julian Ursyn Niemcewicz (1758-1841), the writer, playwright and Kosciuszko-era statesman, who built a library there and was visited in 1830 by the poet Juliusz Slowacki, who admired the estate; the tree is named for Niemcewicz as a former owner of the grounds, but no source dates the tree's planting to his ownership specifically, so age is left undocumented rather than bridged from his 1822-1832ish tenure. The palace passed through several owners after Niemcewicz and has belonged to SGGW (Warsaw University of Life Sciences) since 1956; a 2023-dated photo of a natural monument black walnut at this palace exists on Wikimedia Commons ('Pomnik przyrody orzech czarny rosnacy przy palacu Krasinskich w Warszawie 2023.jpg'), which is evidence of the tree standing as recently as 2023. Access confirmed via the same Wikipedia article and independent local press (haloursynow.pl, iursynow.pl, tvn24.pl, sggw.edu.pl) all reporting the terraced garden behind the palace, where the register places the tree, opened free to the public daily April-October from 2025 after nine years of campaigning; entrance is behind the rector's building at Nowoursynowska 166. Story angle: named for one of Poland's most notable Enlightenment-era statesmen and writers, a companion of Tadeusz Kosciuszko, standing on grounds only recently reopened to the public after being closed university property for decades.
